author: @icy1007

text: @icy1007  no it isnt lol. Theyre both TU104 chips. The difference is the 2080 non-super has bios-disabled smu's. It's literally the same situation as the rx 400 and 500 series. You can flash a rx4xx to the rx5xx of the same tier. A 460 to a 560, 480 to 580 etc. Same chip, more smu's enabled.
author: @BenFilley

text: @Fiklm my 2080 memory hits 16. Im striking distance on overall performance of the 2080S. I also have the msi gaming x trio though, and its a beast. Frankly id settle for a bios that allowed more power limit than the 109 we get out of the box. I think i could match the super with my 2080 with higher tdp.as it sits its got access to 375w given the connectors and the pcie slot. But it only ever pulls 280-285w max.
author: @BenFilley

text: @Fiklm again though I'm just mostly interested in unlocked cores over the memory bump. Yeah that would be nice for the ones that were capable, but the cores are what im looking at. Whether the original 2080 die is limited through the bios, or if its at the silicon level. Its safe to say that if its the exact same silicon as the die name suggests, that the bios should open things up. At that point you can downlock the memory to 14 if you need to for stability, while still opening more cores.  You can also assume the reason they would have some locked away on the original 2080 would have been as simple as the process not having as high a yield in the working core sections across entire batches of chips, so they locked away some via bios and unlocked them later when the process had matured enough to get the yields of higher cores that they wanted. Which is where the super cards come in. Matured process, higher yields. You can assume many would not be up to the task though, I get that. Which is why we need a higher tdp bios for almost all 2080 cards.
